About this guide

What Self & Other is, whom it is for, how it was made, and what it can and cannot do for you.

  • Written forCurious adults, no biology needed
  • Length12 chapters and an interlude, about 5 hours
  • Current as ofOctober 2026
  • Made byAI agents (Anthropic’s Claude), from published sources

Who it is for

Self & Other is for anyone who wants to understand the immune system, and the cancer treatments built on it, without a background in biology. That includes patients and their partners trying to follow what the oncologist said, engineers who want to know how a cell can “decide” anything, and journalists, students and policy makers who keep meeting words like checkpoint inhibitor and CAR-T.

The guide assumes no memory of high-school biology. It explains what a protein, a receptor or a gene does and builds each idea from the ground up. It uses the same scientific terms as research papers and the news, and defines each one the first time it appears. The aim is that specialists find nothing wrong in it, and perhaps a few new things in the “Go deeper” boxes.

How to use it

Read it in order if you can. Part I explains how the immune system works; Part II, what cancer is and how it evades the immune system; Part III, how immunotherapy turns the immune system against it. Each chapter assumes the ones before it, and links back whenever an earlier idea returns. A short interlude tells the history in between.

Every chapter is built in layers, so you can go as deep as you like:

  • The main text. An essay of about 25 minutes that stands on its own.
  • Interactive figures. Each one shows a single idea that is easier to see than to read. You can step through them, drag them or switch between views.
  • “Go deeper” boxes. Molecular names, numbers, history and open questions, folded away until you open them.
  • Glossary. Dotted words show a definition when you hover, focus or tap them; the glossary collects them all.
  • Sources. Small numbers lead to the research behind each claim; every chapter ends with its list, and the sources page gathers them.

Each chapter closes with a few takeaways and a short quiz, for checking yourself rather than for a grade. The site works on phones, in light and dark themes (the button in the header switches them), and it respects your system’s “reduce motion” setting.

How it was made

Everything here, from the text and the interactive figures to the illustrations and this page, was researched, written, drawn and fact-checked by AI agents: instances of Claude, a family of AI models made by Anthropic, working as a team in different roles.

Writers drafted each chapter from published scientific literature, favoring landmark papers and authoritative reviews, and from regulatory sources such as drug approvals and clinical-trial registries. Separate reviewers checked the drafts for scientific accuracy and for clarity to a newcomer, and the drafts were revised in response. Builders then turned them into pages and figures, which were checked again on phones and desktops, in both themes.

Every factual claim is meant to be traceable: the small numbers in the text link to the sources behind it. Results that were known only from a company announcement, not yet from a peer-reviewed paper, are labeled as such. The guide reflects what was known as of October 2026, and medicine moves fast.

Errors are possible

AI systems make mistakes, sometimes confidently. The process above was designed to catch them, but it cannot promise to have caught them all. Treat this guide as a well-sourced starting point: when a detail matters to you, follow the link and read the primary source, or ask someone who works in the field.

Not medical advice

This guide explains how things work. It cannot tell you what to do, and nothing in it is medical advice. Please do not use it to choose, start, stop or change any treatment.

Whether a particular immunotherapy suits a particular person depends on the type, stage and biology of the cancer, on earlier treatments, on other conditions, and on much else that only a care team can weigh. If you or someone you love has cancer, take your questions to the oncologist; the guide may help you work out which questions to ask. And be wary of clinics that sell unproven “immunotherapies” outside of clinical trials.

Finding a clinical trial

New treatments are tested in clinical trials, and joining one can open access to therapies that are not yet approved. The best place to start is a conversation with your oncologist. If you want to search yourself:

  • ClinicalTrials.gov, run by the U.S. National Library of Medicine, lists studies from around the world. You can search by condition, treatment and location.
  • In the United States, the National Cancer Institute offers a cancer clinical trial search and free help by phone at 1-800-4-CANCER.
  • In the European Union, trials are listed in the Clinical Trials Information System.
  • The World Health Organization’s International Clinical Trials Registry Platform searches registries from many countries at once.

A listing is not an endorsement. Eligibility rules are strict and often technical, so ask your care team to help you read them.

A note on the art

The pictures follow one visual idea, the luminous microscope: the pages look like warm paper for reading, and the figures show cells and molecules glowing against a dark background. Each kind of cell keeps one color everywhere in the guide:

  • Killer (CD8) T cells, electric blue
  • Helper (CD4) T cells, teal
  • Healthy body cells, sand
  • Cancer cells, violet
  • B cells and antibodies, gold
  • Dendritic cells, green
  • Macrophages, coral
  • Foreign or mutated peptides, hot pink

Inhibitory signals (brakes) are crimson and carry a bar sign; activating signals are green and carry a plus. Color never works alone: every distinction is also made by shape, a symbol or a label, so the figures read in grayscale and for color-blind readers too. Cells never have faces.

Real cells are neither this tidy nor this colorful. These are diagrams, simplified on purpose, and their scale is often stretched so that molecules a few millionths of a millimeter across can sit next to whole cells.
